raw_response.country: United States (primary focus; brief secondary discussion of United Kingdom, Colombia, and Mexico)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household running water and sewerage service access, specifically residential water service shutoffs (disconnections) for unpaid bills and lack of running water in US cities.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines municipal water utility governance, welfare-state policy, and regulatory interventions. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it focuses directly on rule-type mechanisms governing household water access: utility arrears disconnection/shutoff enforcement rules and cost-recovery policies, state and municipal COVID-19 shutoff moratoria, utility debt-relief and income-based billing rules (Portland's Afloat program and Philadelphia's Tiered Assistance Program [TAP]), categorical disconnection exemptions and self-identification documentation waivers (Philadelphia's 'Raise Your Hand' initiative requiring no documentation), and property-ownership rules barring renters from opening water accounts in Baltimore.
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis. The paper is the published text of an invited plenary lecture (2023 RGS-IBG Political Geography Lecture; received 12 Feb 2024 and accepted 13 Feb 2024) advancing a theoretical argument anchored in social reproduction and carceral state scholarship. The author explicitly states that the empirical findings from the lecture were published separately with collaborators (Meehan et al., under review) and characterizes the present piece as an essay pursuing a theoretical line of argumentation. City vignettes (Portland, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Detroit) rely on secondary news reporting (Kent, 2023; Walton, 2018, 2020; Schmidt, 2023; Wilson, 2015), a screenshot of a promotional YouTube video (Fig. 2), and a descriptive map of NARUC state moratorium dates (Fig. 3) with no empirical methods section, sampling design, or systematic review protocol. Excluded as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses outcomes directly relevant to household water access, exclusion/disconnection, service restoration, and affordability/arrears (e.g., weekly/monthly shutoff counts, reconnections, households without running water, and unpaid bill balances reported in secondary sources).
criterion_notes.c5: Although target populations, rule-type exposures, and access/disconnection outcomes are discussed conceptually and via secondary journalism, the paper lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sample frame, or data-collection/analytic method (failing Inclusion Criterion 7 / c5).

evidence_quotes.quote: Through an investigation of shutoff practices in US cities, the article finds that access to safe and secure running water is increasingly weaponized as a “police structure” to preserve a model of debt-driven water management, in ways that also produce a spatial and racial division of nature.

Like most water utilities in the USA, the Portland Water Bureau will suspend water service to customers who are behind on their bills. Shutoffs, as service disconnections are colloquially known, are a legal and routine practice at the more than 50,000 water utilities across the United States (Walton, 2018).

Customers the Water Department has not already identified as protected from shutoffs through its data matching efforts can contact the Water Department through a new ‘Raise Your Hand’ initiative, which allows families facing disconnection to self-identify as a protected category with no documentation required.

Part of these ideas were first presented in the Political Geography Lecture at the Royal Geographical Society-Institute of British Geographers (RGS-IBG) Annual Lecture in August 2023; I thank the organizers, commentators, and audience members for their keen insights and feedback.

Some of the major findings and data visualizations I presented in that lecture have since been published in a joint paper elsewhere with my collaborators (Meehan et al., under review). In this essay, I want to pursue a more specified line of argumentation centered on the changing nature of the welfare state and its relationship to households.
In total, some 15,500 customers in Portland are behind on their water and sewer bills, with only 4200 (27%) on payment plans
